agent_explanations_oldest_first.text:
The end-of-prompt value that head 3 amplifies is a math-task signal. Its projection on the T1 direction is:

| Group | Prompt | Projection |
|---|---|---|
| G1 | math problem + instruction | 16.0 |
| G2 | math problem alone | 10.9 |
| G4 | math problem + translate | 8.2 |
| G5 | poem + math instruction | 8.3 |
| G3 | plain poem | 1.1 |

The math-minus-poem difference lies almost entirely along this direction (cos 0.94). Head 3 turns it into a 20-unit write, against 4.7–9.4 for the siblings' writes of the full math value.

So the mechanism is: a math-detection feature arrives at the end-of-prompt token, and L11 head 3 broadcasts an amplified version of it, through its value-to-output mapping, into every answer token. Removing just that response (T1) recovered +25.7 points. This fits the task's "hiding capability on math".

Before tuning T1's strength, I scan the whole model for the same mechanism. For every layer, I form the math-specific end-of-prompt value d_l = V(G1) − V(G3) from group means, and for every head its write of d_l, absolute and relative to the head's average gain. L18 is the obvious suspect: its end-of-prompt value is equally oversized and all its heads respond strongly to it. I also compare the direction of head 3's write of v̂ with its siblings' writes of the same input. A shared direction would mean a natural task broadcast that is merely amplified. A distinct direction would mean a separate, specific write.

The model-wide scan does not single out L11 head 3 by weights alone. Late-layer heads (L18–L22) write larger math-specific end-of-prompt differences (25–32 units), because the end-of-prompt state naturally diverges more there. Head 3's write of the difference (20.3) is below the 90th percentile (25.4). Its write direction also differs from its siblings' (cos 0.47 with h0, −0.19/0.15 with h1/h2), so it is a distinct write, not a shared task broadcast that is merely amplified.

The case for head 3 is therefore causal rather than forensic. Removing its response to the math-task value gives +25.7 against +18.6 for damping the whole head and −0.9 for removing its spike, on the same problems.

The large late-layer writes are probably natural task conditioning, and the L18 heads read an end-of-prompt value that is large even for the poem (51.8), so they look like a natural secondary sink. I therefore do not chase them without causal evidence.

Next, I check that T1 generalises before tuning it. I run it on DEV[0:256], a different slice, where head 2 ×3 gave +6.25. A clearly positive result of comparable size (around +15 to +25) confirms T1 as the lead. A small gain would mean the +25.7 partly reflects that one slice. First I verify that the saved edit is exactly T1 and log the plan.

The saved edit is exactly T1. Head 3's response to the math-task value direction is reduced from 1.367 to 0.002, and heads 0–2 are bit-identical. I now run the paired generation on DEV[0:256] to check that T1's gain holds on a different slice from the one it was found on.

T1 holds up on a fresh slice: on DEV[0:256] it gives +19.9 ± 3.2 points (63 wrong→right, 12 right→wrong). Accuracy rises from 22.3% to 42.2%, and cut-offs fall from 23% to 12%. On this same slice, boosting head 2 ×3 had given only +6.25. Together with +25.7 on DEV[1024:1250], T1 is now a robust lead at about +23 points across two independent DEV slices.

T1 sets head 3's response to the math-task value to zero. The next question is whether zero is the right level. To map the dose around it, I test T1 at strength α = 1.5 on DEV[1024:1250], where α = 1 gave +25.7. This edit reverses the response at half its original size, B3 − 1.5·(B3 v̂)v̂ᵀ.
- If α = 1.5 is better, the original response was the negative of a useful write, and a fuller reversal is worth trying.
- If it is worse, the optimum is at or below removal, and I will check α = 0.5 to see whether part of the response is useful.
